title: Best Practices & Common Pitfalls 💡
description: Handle SSDs, encrypted drives, HPA regions, and document everything like a pro.

slides.title: The SSD Challenge ⚡
slides.content:
# Solid‑State Drives: Different Rules

SSDs are not like spinning disks. Key differences:

- **TRIM**: OS tells SSD to wipe blocks of deleted files, making recovery harder.
- **Garbage Collection**: Background process that erases invalid pages.
- **Wear Leveling**: Logical block addresses (LBAs) do not map to fixed physical locations.

**Imaging SSDs**: Use a physical acquisition as soon as possible. Even with a write blocker, the SSD's internal controller may still modify data in the background, but this doesn't change the logical data you read at that moment. Hash verification still works.

quizData.question: A hardware write blocker can prevent all internal changes on an SSD, including garbage collection.
quizData.explanation: A write blocker stops writes from the host, but it cannot stop the SSD's own controller from performing background operations like garbage collection.

slides.title: Encrypted Drives 🔐
slides.content:
## Full‑Disk Encryption (FDE)

If a drive is encrypted (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS), you cannot read the data without the key. During acquisition:

- If the system is **live and unlocked**, capture a memory dump and a logical image of the unlocked volume.
- If the system is **off**, image the encrypted drive as a physical raw image. Later, attempt to obtain the key (from suspect, TPM chip, or via legal process).

Never attempt to decrypt by brute‑forcing during acquisition – just image it and preserve the state.

quizData.question: What is the recommended action when you encounter a powered‑off laptop with BitLocker encryption?

options.text: Turn it on and log in to decrypt
Remove the drive, image it with a write blocker, and preserve the encrypted state
Format the drive to remove encryption

quizData.explanation: Never power on an encrypted device; you may lose the ability to decrypt. Image the drive as‑is and work on obtaining the key later.

slides.title: Host Protected Area (HPA) & DCO 🕳️
slides.content:
A drive can be configured to report a smaller capacity than its actual size. The hidden area is called:

- **HPA (Host Protected Area)**: Set via ATA command, hides sectors at the end.
- **DCO (Device Configuration Overlay)**: Hides features or sectors, often used by manufacturers.

Criminals have used HPA to hide data. Use tools like `hdparm` or specialized forensic tools to detect and temporarily remove HPA for imaging.

```bash
hdparm -N /dev/sda   # Check HPA status
hdparm -N p<max> /dev/sda  # Temporarily remove HPA (risky!)
```

quizData.question: A drive's physical size as reported by `fdisk` is always its true maximum capacity.
quizData.explanation: HPA and DCO can make the drive report a smaller size, hiding sectors. Always check with `hdparm` or forensic tools.

slides.title: Documentation During Acquisition 📋
slides.content:
Your contemporaneous notes are vital. Record:

- Make, model, serial number of the evidence drive.
- Tool used (name, version).
- Write blocker make/model/serial.
- Hash algorithm and values.
- Date, time, location.
- Any anomalies (strange noises, errors).

Take screenshots or photos of each step. These become part of the chain of custody and report.

slides.title: Example Acquisition Log Entry
slides.content: A markdown sample log entry for your case notes.
slides.codeSnippet:
**Acquisition Log – Case #2026‑045**
- Date: 2026‑05‑10 09:15 UTC
- Evidence Drive: Seagate ST1000LM048, S/N: Z7F3A9BQ
- Write Blocker: Tableau T35u, S/N: TB2105, tested 2026‑05‑01
- Tool: dcfldd v1.3.4
- Image file: /mnt/evidence/case045.dd
- Source SHA‑256: ab12... (full hash)
- Image SHA‑256: ab12... (matches)
- Notes: No errors. Drive imaged in 1h 12m.

slides.title: ⚠️ Avoid Common Mistakes
slides.content:
- **Forgetting to test the write blocker**.
- **Not hashing before and after**.
- **Using USB hubs** that may interfere with write‑blocker commands.
- **Booting the suspect machine accidentally**.
- **Storing the image on an unencrypted drive** (case data must be protected).

quizData.question: Why should you avoid using a USB hub during forensic imaging?

options.text: It may bypass write‑blocker protections or introduce errors

quizData.explanation: Some hubs do not pass through certain SCSI/ATA commands correctly, potentially allowing writes to slip through.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Mirror the Image

Immediately after acquisition, create a working copy of the image. Keep the master image pristine and only analyse the copy. If something goes wrong, you still have the original image.
